claim: Single strong body bends on one side of the body, also known as coils, emerge during the first day of development at around 17 hr post-fertilization (hpf) as the earliest locomotor behavior.
source: Single strong body bends on one side of the body, also known as coils, emerge during the first day of development at around 17 hr post-fertilization (hpf) as the earliest locomotor behavior (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998.

claim: Single coils are quickly followed by double coils (i.e., two successive coils, one for each side of the body) at around 24 hpf.
source: Single coils are quickly followed by double coils (i.e., two successive coils, one for each side of the body) at around 24 hpf (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Touch-evoked swimming appears around 27 hpf as coiling begins to subside.
source: Touch-evoked swimming appears around 27 hpf as coiling begins to subside.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text without supporting data or citation in this sentence.

claim: Spontaneous swimming movements emerge around 2–3 days post-fertilization (dpf).
source: Spontaneous swimming movements emerge around 2–3 days post-fertilization (dpf) (Saint-Amant, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant, 2010.

claim: The first swimming movement zebrafish exhibit is burst swimming characterized by long (1 s long) but infrequent episodes of tail beats.
source: The first swimming movement zebrafish exhibit is burst swimming characterized by long (1 s long) but infrequent episodes of tail beats.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Burst swimming is then replaced by beat-and-glide swimming characterized by shorter (several hundreds of milliseconds long) but more frequent episodes.
source: Burst swimming is then replaced by beat-and-glide swimming characterized by shorter (several hundreds of milliseconds long) but more frequent episodes.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Swim episodes consist of repetitive left-right alternating, low-amplitude tail beats that propagate from the rostral toward the caudal end of the fish body and are generated at 20 to 80 Hz.
source: In both cases, swim episodes consist of repetitive left-right alternating, low-amplitude tail beats that propagate from the rostral toward the caudal end of the fish body and are generated at 20 to 80 Hz (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Buss and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budick and O'Malley, 2000 and Buss and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Primary motoneurons (MNs) are generated at about 9 hpf.
source: During this rapid series of transitions between locomotor maneuvers, populations of spinal neurons are progressively generated, starting with primary motoneurons (MNs) at about 9 hpf.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Spinal MNs and interneurons (INs) are generated in stereotyped spatiotemporal birth orders.
source: Subsequently, spinal MNs and interneurons (INs) are generated in stereotyped spatiotemporal birth orders (Kimmel et al., 1994; Myers et al., 1986; Satou et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimmel et al., 1994; Myers et al., 1986; Satou et al., 2012.

claim: Two successive waves of axogenesis occur in the embryonic spinal cord.
source: Two successive waves of axogenesis occur in the embryonic spinal cord (Bernhardt et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bernhardt et al., 1990.

claim: The first wave of axogenesis occurs around 16–17 hpf.
source: The first wave occurs around 16–17 hpf.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The first wave of axogenesis includes axon growth in primary MNs that innervate red and white muscle fibers at early developmental stages.
source: It includes axon growth in primary MNs that innervate red and white muscle fibers at early developmental stages (Buss and Drapeau, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buss and Drapeau, 2000.

claim: Primary MNs enable coiling and escape movements.
source: Primary MNs enable coiling and escape movements (Kimmel et al., 1995; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimmel et al., 1995 and Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000.

claim: Ipsilateral Caudal (IC) INs are thought to play an essential role in driving the rhythm of early locomotor behavior due to their endogenous bursting activity.
source: These include Ipsilateral Caudal (IC) INs that are thought to play an essential role in driving the rhythm of early locomotor behavior due to their endogenous bursting activity (Tong and McDearmid, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tong and McDearmid, 2012.

claim: The second wave of axon growth occurs at around 23–25 hpf.
source: The second wave of axon growth occurs at around 23–25 hpf.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The second wave of axon growth involves axon growth in secondary MNs involved with slower movements.
source: It involves axon growth in secondary MNs involved with slower movements (Liu and Westerfield, 1988) and spinal IN populations that include excitatory and inhibitory, ipsilaterally and contralaterally, and ascending and descending projecting subtypes (Bernhardt et al., 1990; Higashijima et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Westerfield, 1988; Bernhardt et al., 1990; Higashijima et al., 2004.

claim: The progressive generation of new populations of spinal neurons and continued axonal growth coincides with the expansion of the zebrafish locomotor repertoire.
source: The progressive generation of new populations of spinal neurons and continued axonal growth coincides with the expansion of the zebrafish locomotor repertoire.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The maturation from coiling to later stages of swimming is accompanied by an operational switch in how spinal locomotor circuits generate the rhythm underlying tail beats.
source: We have recently provided evidence that the maturation from coiling to later stages of swimming is accompanied by an operational switch in how spinal locomotor circuits generate the rhythm underlying tail beats.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as a finding from the authors' recent work.

claim: Spinal circuits transitioned from relying upon pacemakers with endogenous bursting properties during coiling toward depending upon network oscillators whose rhythm is driven by excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that spinal circuits transitioned from relying upon pacemakers with endogenous bursting properties during coiling toward depending upon network oscillators whose rhythm is driven by excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Roussel et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roussel et al., 2020.

claim: Coiling is characterized by a single strong, slow (hundreds of milliseconds in duration) tail beat on one side of the body followed by a return to resting position.
source: Coiling, which is already observed at 1 dpf, is characterized by a single strong, slow (hundreds of milliseconds in duration) tail beat on one side of the body followed by a return to resting position (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998.

claim: Coiling events are relatively infrequent, reaching a maximum frequency of 1 Hz around 20 hpf.
source: Coiling events are relatively infrequent, reaching a maximum frequency of 1 Hz around 20 hpf (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998.

claim: Coiling behavior is generated by a spinal circuit relying primarily on gap junctions (i.e., electrical synapses).
source: Previous studies have established that this behavior is generated by a spinal circuit relying primarily on gap junctions (i.e., electrical synapses) (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Rostrally located IC pacemaker spinal neurons drive periodic depolarizations (PDs) of ipsilateral MNs via electrical synapses.
source: It has been proposed that rostrally located IC pacemaker spinal neurons (Tong and McDearmid, 2012) drive periodic depolarizations (PDs) of ipsilateral MNs via electrical synapses (Drapeau et al., 2002; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tong and McDearmid, 2012; Drapeau et al., 2002; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Glycinergic synaptic bursts (SBs) are observed in MNs during contralateral coiling events.
source: Glycinergic synaptic bursts (SBs) are observed in MNs during contralateral coiling events (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Glycinergic SBs have been proposed to arise from contralaterally projecting glycinergic neurons but are not responsible for any action potential firings or coiling movements.
source: These SBs have been proposed to arise from contralaterally projecting glycinergic neurons (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000) but are not responsible for any action potential firings or coiling movements (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000 and Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Applying a gap junction blocker, heptanol, but not glutamatergic and glycinergic antagonists, suppressed spinal activity responsible for coiling.
source: Applying a gap junction blocker, heptanol, but not glutamatergic and glycinergic antagonists, suppressed spinal activity responsible for coiling (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000.

claim: The single coiling model consisted of rostrocaudal chains of electrically coupled spinal neurons driven by a kernel of five recurrently connected pacemakers (IC neurons).
source: Based on the experimental observations reported above, the model for single coiling consisted of rostrocaudal chains of electrically coupled spinal neurons driven by a kernel of five recurrently connected pacemakers (IC neurons).
evidence: The claim describes the structure of the computational model built by the authors.

claim: Neurons from the V0d population are active during large amplitude movements such as escapes.
source: Neurons from the V0d population are active during large amplitude movements such as escapes (Satou et al., 2020), and so we assumed V0ds were the commissural inhibitory neurons active during coiling, which is another large amplitude movement.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Satou et al., 2020.

claim: The single coiling model generated six evenly interspersed single coils during a 10 s simulation.
source: Our base single coiling model generated six evenly interspersed single coils during a 10 s simulation.
evidence: The claim describes a result from the computational model simulation.

claim: The 0.6 Hz coiling frequency is within the 0–1.0 Hz range of frequencies observed during zebrafish development.
source: This 0.6 Hz coiling frequency is within the 0–1.0 Hz range of frequencies observed during zebrafish development (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998 and Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2000.

claim: Silencing ICs blocked activity in all spinal neurons.
source: Silencing ICs blocked activity in all spinal neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), emphasizing the central role of the IC kernel in the generation of single coils.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Preventing SBs by silencing glycinergic synapses from V0ds did not preclude the generation of single coiling, nor did it lead to the generation of multiple coilings.
source: As observed experimentally (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001), preventing SBs by silencing glycinergic synapses from V0ds did not preclude the generation of single coiling, nor did it lead to the generation of multiple coilings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IC neuron firing precedes ipsilateral MN and V0d firing.
source: An analysis of the phase delays between ipsilateral neurons during single coils shows that IC neuron firing precedes ipsilateral MN and V0d firing (Figure 2E) and reinforces that ICs drive single coiling events.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Double coils emerge as a transitory locomotor behavior at around 24 hpf, coexisting with the single coiling behavior.
source: After single coils appear, double coils emerge as a transitory locomotor behavior at around 24 hpf, coexisting with the single coiling behavior (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Double coiling is characterized by two successive coils, one on each side of the body, and lasts about 1 s.
source: Double coiling is characterized by two successive coils, one on each side of the body, and lasts about 1 s (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Double coiling can represent nearly three-quarters of all coiling events at its peak frequency.
source: Double coiling can represent nearly three-quarters of all coiling events at its peak frequency, with the rest mainly being single coils (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: At the stage when double coiling appears (24 dpf), the previous electrical scaffold for single coils seems to be supplemented with chemical glutamatergic synapses to form a hybrid electrical-chemical circuit.
source: At the stage when double coiling appears (24 dpf), the previous electrical scaffold for single coils seems to be supplemented with chemical glutamatergic synapses to form a hybrid electrical-chemical circuit (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking glutamatergic transmission precludes double coils while sparing single coils.
source: Blocking glutamatergic transmission precludes double coils while sparing single coils (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking glycinergic synapses led to triple or even quadruple coils.
source: In contrast, blocking glycinergic synapses led to triple or even quadruple coils (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: The application of CNQX eliminates mixed PD-SB events but not single isolated SBs, suggesting that the coupling of PD and SB in mixed events is glutamatergic.
source: Interestingly, the application of CNQX eliminates mixed PD-SB events but not single isolated SBs, suggesting that the coupling of PD and SB in mixed events is glutamatergic (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Blocking glutamatergic transmission in the double coiling model greatly reduced the number of double coils.
source: To further underscore the importance of glutamatergic transmission to double coiling as reported experimentally (Knogler et al., 2014), blocking glutamatergic transmission in the model greatly reduced the number of double coils (Figure 3F,I, Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 3F,I.

claim: Blocking glycinergic synapses in the double coiling model increased multiple coilings of three or more coils.
source: On the other hand, blocking glycinergic synapses increased multiple coilings of three or more coils (Figure 3G,I, Figure 3—video 4) as Knogler et al., 2014 reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 3G,I.

claim: Around 2 or 3 dpf, zebrafish transition from coiling movements to swimming.
source: Around 2 or 3 dpf, zebrafish transition from coiling movements to swimming (Drapeau et al., 2002; Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Drapeau et al., 2002 and Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 1998.

claim: Beat-and-glide swimming is characterized by short swimming episodes lasting several hundreds of milliseconds separated by gliding pauses and lasting several hundreds of milliseconds.
source: One of the emerging swimming movements is beat-and-glide swimming, characterized by short swimming episodes lasting several hundreds of milliseconds separated by gliding pauses and lasting several hundreds of milliseconds (Budick and O'Malley, 2000; Buss and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Budick and O'Malley, 2000 and Buss and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Beat-and-glide swimming can be produced in isolated larval zebrafish spinal cord preparations by NMDA application.
source: Beat-and-glide swimming can be produced in isolated larval zebrafish spinal cord preparations by NMDA application (Lambert et al., 2012; McDearmid and Drapeau, 2006; Wiggin et al., 2012) or by optogenetic stimulation of excitatory spinal neurons (Wahlstrom-Helgren et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lambert et al., 2012; McDearmid and Drapeau, 2006; Wiggin et al., 2012.

claim: Beat-and-glide swimming can be produced in isolated larval zebrafish spinal cord preparations by optogenetic stimulation of excitatory spinal neurons.
source: Beat-and-glide swimming can be produced in isolated larval zebrafish spinal cord preparations by NMDA application (Lambert et al., 2012; McDearmid and Drapeau, 2006; Wiggin et al., 2012) or by optogenetic stimulation of excitatory spinal neurons (Wahlstrom-Helgren et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wahlstrom-Helgren et al., 2019.

claim: Ablation of ipsilaterally projecting, excitatory neurons in the V2a population eliminates swimming activity.
source: Ablation of ipsilaterally projecting, excitatory neurons in the V2a population eliminates swimming activity (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012.

claim: Genetic ablation of ipsilaterally projecting, inhibitory neurons in the V1 population affects swim vigor but has no effects on the patterning of swimming.
source: Genetic ablation of ipsilaterally projecting, inhibitory neurons in the V1 population affects swim vigor but has no effects on the patterning of swimming (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kimura and Higashijima, 2019.

claim: Genetic ablation of a subset of commissural inhibitory neurons in the dI6 population reduces left-right alternation.
source: Genetic ablation of a subset of commissural inhibitory neurons in the dI6 population reduces left-right alternation (Satou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Satou et al., 2020.

claim: The beat-and-glide swimming model exhibited short-duration (hundreds of milliseconds) swimming episodes with left-right alternation and tail beat frequencies between 20 and 60 Hz.
source: The beat-and-glide swimming model exhibited short-duration (hundreds of milliseconds) swimming episodes with left-right alternation and tail beat frequencies between 20 and 60 Hz (Figure 4C–G, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–G.

claim: Silencing V2as abolished the generation of tail beats.
source: Silencing V2as abolished the generation of tail beats (Figure 5A–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F), underscoring their primacy to the generation of tail beats (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Ljunggren et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012 and Ljunggren et al., 2014, and data shown in Figure 5A–F.

claim: Silencing V0vs diminished but did not eliminate the rhythmic firing of V2as or MNs.
source: Silencing V0vs diminished but did not eliminate the rhythmic firing of V2as or MNs.
evidence: The claim describes a result from the computational model simulation.

claim: Removing the contralateral excitation by V0v prevented the repetitive activation of the silent side after each tail beat, which severely reduced episode duration and the number of tail beats generated in each episode.
source: However, removing the contralateral excitation by V0v prevented the repetitive activation of the silent side after each tail beat, which severely reduced episode duration and the number of tail beats generated in each episode (Figure 5G–L, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–L, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G–L.

claim: Simulating the removal of ipsilateral ascending inhibition by silencing V1 INs seemed to increase the amplitude of MN activity.
source: Consistent with those experimental results, simulating the removal of ipsilateral ascending inhibition by silencing V1 INs seemed to increase the amplitude of MN activity (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F, Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Silencing V1 INs increased the duration of episodes and shortened inter-episode intervals.
source: While the overall beat-and-glide pattern persisted, the duration of episodes was increased, and inter-episode intervals were shortened between epochs 1 and 2 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Silencing V1 INs increased tail beat frequency.
source: Tail beat frequency was increased (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Left-right alternation was reduced during simulations where dI6s were silenced.
source: Left-right alternation was reduced in these simulations and during simulations where dI6s were silenced (Figure 6F,G,L, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F,G,L.

claim: The reduction in left-right alternation during simulations where dI6s were silenced was greater in caudal somites than in rostral somites.
source: The reduction in left-right alternation during simulations where dI6s were silenced was greater in caudal somites than in rostral somites (Figure 6L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Silencing dI6s had negligible effects on the episode duration and inter-episode interval but increased tail beat frequency.
source: Finally, silencing dI6s had negligible effects on the episode duration and inter-episode interval but increased tail beat frequency when comparing epochs 1 and 2 and may increase the amplitude of motor activity (Figure 6H–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6H–K.

claim: Removal of all glycinergic transmission led to continual tail beats with minimal gliding periods.
source: Removal of all glycinergic transmission led to continual tail beats with minimal gliding periods (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Motor output was increased during the epoch of no glycinergic transmission.
source: Motor output was increased during the epoch of no glycinergic transmission (Figure 7B), episode duration was considerably lengthened, and the inter-episode interval was shortened (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Removing glycinergic transmission increased the frequency of tail beats.
source: The frequency of tail beats increased (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Removing glycinergic transmission reduced left-right alternation, particularly at caudal somites.
source: Left-right alternation was reduced, particularly at caudal somites (Figure 7F), which did not preclude left-right tail beats but altered swimming kinematics (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A model with bursting V2as generated 100–400 ms swimming episodes of left-right alternating tail beats at frequencies around 20–80 Hz interspersed by 100–400 ms long silent inter-episode intervals.
source: A model with bursting V2as where we also decreased the strength of synapses from V2as to other neurons and increased the connection strength of V0vs and dI6s to contralateral V2as (Table 3) generated 100–400 ms swimming episodes of left-right alternating tail beats at frequencies around 20–80 Hz interspersed by 100–400 ms long silent inter-episode intervals (Figure 8B–F, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–F.

claim: A model with only tonic firing neurons was able to generate the hallmarks of beat-and-glide swimming.
source: Surprisingly, a model with only tonic firing neurons (Figure 8G) was able to generate the hallmarks of beat-and-glide swimming as well (Figure 8H–L, Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8G–L.

claim: Episode duration was increased, and inter-episode intervals decreased at more depolarized values of the glycinergic reversal potential leading to the loss of the beat-and-glide pattern.
source: Episode duration was increased, and inter-episode intervals decreased at more depolarized values of the glycinergic reversal potential leading to the loss of the beat-and-glide pattern (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Tail beat frequency increased as glycinergic currents decreased at depolarized glycinergic reversal potentials, and left-right alternation was replaced by left-right synchrony.
source: Tail beat frequency also increased as glycinergic currents decreased at depolarized glycinergic reversal potentials, and left-right alternation was replaced by left-right synchrony (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The single coiling model is more robust to noise in the amplitude of the tonic motor command and was most sensitive to variability in the parameters governing the dynamics of the membrane potential.
source: A comparison of the level of variability at which the models start generating more varying frequency of coiling and more truncated coils suggests that the single coiling model is more robust to noise in the amplitude of the tonic motor command (Figure 2F, J) and was most sensitive to variability in the parameters governing the dynamics of the membrane potential (Figure 2H, L).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F, J, H, L.

claim: The single coiling model was relatively mildly sensitive to variability in the synaptic weights and the rostrocaudal extent of the axon projections.
source: The single coiling model was relatively mildly sensitive to variability in the synaptic weights and the rostrocaudal extent of the axon projections (Figure 2G, I, K, M).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G, I, K, M.

claim: The proportion of double coils was relatively more sensitive to the variability of gap junctions than chemical synapses.
source: We found that the proportion of double coils was relatively more sensitive to the variability of gap junctions than chemical synapses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The beat-and-glide model was most susceptible to variations in the parameters determining membrane potential dynamics and similarly sensitive to the other parameters tested.
source: Thus, the beat-and-glide model was most susceptible to variations in the parameters determining membrane potential dynamics and similarly sensitive to the other parameters tested.
evidence: The claim summarizes the sensitivity analysis results for the beat-and-glide model.

claim: The double coiling model predicts that the generation of double and even multiple coils depend on untested connections between V2a and V0v neurons and between V0v and IC neurons.
source: Our modeling study also predicts that the generation of double and even multiple coils depend on untested connections between V2a and V0v neurons and between V0v and IC neurons.
evidence: The claim is a prediction made by the authors based on their modeling results.

claim: The V2a to V0v connection could be deemed unnecessary in light of possible gap junction coupling between ipsilateral IC and V0vs.
source: The V2a to V0v connection could be deemed unnecessary in light of possible gap junction coupling between ipsilateral IC and V0vs.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Delayed activation of V0vs would allow the ipsilateral coil to complete before activating the contralateral coil.
source: However, our modeling suggests that delayed activation of V0vs would allow the ipsilateral coil to complete before activating the contralateral coil.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The double-coiling model predicts that contralateral inhibition of ICs by V0ds prevents the generation of multiple coilings.
source: Our double-coiling model also predicts that contralateral inhibition of ICs by V0ds prevents the generation of multiple coilings.
evidence: The claim is a prediction made by the authors based on their modeling results.

claim: The beat-and-glide model proposes a prominent role of delayed contralateral excitation in ensuring repetitive left-right alternating tail beats during swimming.
source: The beat-and-glide model also proposes a prominent role of delayed contralateral excitation in ensuring repetitive left-right alternating tail beats during swimming.
evidence: The claim is a proposal made by the authors based on their modeling results.

claim: Different subgroups of V0v neurons are probably involved in coiling versus swimming.
source: While V0v neurons are the likely candidate to mediate the activation of contralateral movements, different subgroups of V0v neurons are probably involved in coiling versus swimming (Björnfors and El Manira, 2016; Jay and McLean, 2019) considering the two different targets of contralateral excitation involved, namely ICs in coiling and V2as in swimming.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Björnfors and El Manira, 2016 and Jay and McLean, 2019.

claim: The ability of the model to generate beat-and-glide swimming with or without burst firing neurons suggests a possible degeneracy in the operation of spinal swimming circuits of the developing zebrafish.
source: Finally, the ability of our model to generate beat-and-glide swimming with or without burst firing neurons suggests a possible degeneracy in the operation of spinal swimming circuits of the developing zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Coiling is likely to be generated by primary MNs.
source: Whereas coiling is likely to be generated by primary MNs, swimming is more likely to involve secondary MNs (Ampatzis et al., 2013; Liu and Westerfield, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ampatzis et al., 2013 and Liu and Westerfield, 1988.

claim: Swimming is more likely to involve secondary MNs.
source: Whereas coiling is likely to be generated by primary MNs, swimming is more likely to involve secondary MNs (Ampatzis et al., 2013; Liu and Westerfield, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ampatzis et al., 2013 and Liu and Westerfield, 1988.

claim: Commissural inhibitory CoBL neurons (including neurons from the dI6 and V0d populations) are active during swimming.
source: Commissural inhibitory CoBL neurons (including neurons from the dI6 and V0d populations) are active during swimming (Liao and Fetcho, 2008; Satou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liao and Fetcho, 2008 and Satou et al., 2020.

claim: V0d neurons were involved with faster swimming, whereas dI6s were more likely to be active during slower swimming.
source: V0d neurons were involved with faster swimming, whereas dI6s were more likely to be active during slower swimming (Satou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Satou et al., 2020.

claim: CoBL neurons have been shown to project to MNs, dI6s, and unidentified ipsilateral descending spinal neurons that could be V2as.
source: CoBL neurons have been shown to project to MNs, dI6s, and unidentified ipsilateral descending spinal neurons that could be V2as (Satou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Satou et al., 2020.

claim: V1 neurons were not included in the coiling models because their role in that form of movement is unclear.
source: While V1 neurons were not included in the coiling models because their role in that form of movement is unclear, experiments in which the genetically identified V1 neurons are ablated suggest a role in controlling swim vigor (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: Experiments in which the genetically identified V1 neurons are ablated suggest a role in controlling swim vigor.
source: While V1 neurons were not included in the coiling models because their role in that form of movement is unclear, experiments in which the genetically identified V1 neurons are ablated suggest a role in controlling swim vigor (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kimura and Higashijima, 2019.

claim: V2as were considered the primary source of rhythmogenesis in the models of beat-and-glide swimming based on previous studies showing the necessity and sufficiency of V2a neurons to swimming activity.
source: V2as were considered the primary source of rhythmogenesis in our models of beat-and-glide swimming based on previous studies showing the necessity and sufficiency of V2a neurons to swimming activity (Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012; Ljunggren et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eklöf-Ljunggren et al., 2012 and Ljunggren et al., 2014.

claim: Connections between V2as and V2as have been reported.
source: Connections between V2as and V2as (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020) and from V2a neurons to MNs (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020) have been reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020.

claim: Connections from V2a neurons to MNs have been reported.
source: Connections between V2as and V2as (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020) and from V2a neurons to MNs (Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020) have been reported.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ampatzis et al., 2014; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Song et al., 2020.

claim: A subtype of V2a neurons that project to MNs was shown to bifurcate and have short ascending branches.
source: A subtype of V2a neurons that project to MNs was shown to bifurcate and have short ascending branches (Menelaou and McLean, 2019), which we modeled in addition to an ascending V2a to V0v connection (the ith V2a projected to rostral V0vs and MNs in the i−1 and i−2 segments) that remains to be confirmed.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Menelaou and McLean, 2019.

claim: In adult zebrafish, V0v commissural excitatory neurons have been shown to have bifurcating axons with shorter ascending branches and longer descending branches.
source: However, in adult zebrafish, V0v commissural excitatory neurons have been shown to have bifurcating axons with shorter ascending branches and longer descending branches (Björnfors and El Manira, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Björnfors and El Manira, 2016.

claim: There is evidence for rhythmic and tonic activity in reticulospinal neurons involved in swimming.
source: There is evidence for rhythmic and tonic activity in reticulospinal neurons involved in swimming (Kimura et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kimura et al., 2013.

claim: The isolated zebrafish spinal cord can generate rhythmic activity similar to swimming.
source: However, the isolated zebrafish spinal cord can generate rhythmic activity similar to swimming (McDearmid and Drapeau, 2006; Wahlstrom-Helgren et al., 2019; Wiggin et al., 2012; Wiggin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McDearmid and Drapeau, 2006; Wahlstrom-Helgren et al., 2019; Wiggin et al., 2012; Wiggin et al., 2014.

claim: Most spinal neurons at larval stages exhibit either tonic firing or firing with spike rate adaptation.
source: Most spinal neurons at larval stages exhibit either tonic firing or firing with spike rate adaptation (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019; Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Satou et al., 2020), while a subset of MNs showing intrinsic burst firing (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kimura and Higashijima, 2019; Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Satou et al., 2020.

claim: A subset of MNs show intrinsic burst firing.
source: Most spinal neurons at larval stages exhibit either tonic firing or firing with spike rate adaptation (Kimura and Higashijima, 2019; Menelaou and McLean, 2012; Menelaou and McLean, 2019; Satou et al., 2020), while a subset of MNs showing intrinsic burst firing (Menelaou and McLean, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Menelaou and McLean, 2012.

claim: The activity of ipsilateral, glutamatergic V2as precedes the activity of all ipsilateral neurons during beat-and-glide swimming in the base model.
source: An analysis of the phase delay between neuron populations during beat-and-glide swimming in the base model shows that the activity of ipsilateral, glutamatergic V2as precedes the activity of all ipsilateral neurons (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The glycinergic V1 neurons succeed all ipsilateral spinal neurons, suggesting they provide negative feedback to ipsilateral spinal swimming circuits.
source: On the other hand, the glycinergic V1 neurons succeed all ipsilateral spinal neurons, suggesting they provide negative feedback to ipsilateral spinal swimming circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the phase delay analysis.

claim: The contralateral dI6s and V0vs are out-of-phase with contralateral spinal neurons, consistent with their role in mediating left-right coordination.
source: The contralateral dI6s and V0vs are out-of-phase with contralateral spinal neurons, consistent with their role in mediating left-right coordination.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the phase delay analysis.

claim: The generation of alternating left-right tail beats would seem to require a certain delay in the excitation of contralateral swimming circuits.
source: Thus, the generation of alternating left-right tail beats would seem to require a certain delay in the excitation of contralateral swimming circuits.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Commissural excitation mediated by V0vs seemed to be very important in maintaining the beat-and-glide pattern.
source: Commissural excitation mediated by V0vs seemed to be very important in maintaining the beat-and-glide pattern.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Commissural excitation is necessary to repeatedly activate the silent contralateral side during ongoing swimming to ensure successive left-right alternating tail beats and longer swim episodes.
source: These simulations suggest that commissural excitation is necessary to repeatedly activate the silent contralateral side during ongoing swimming to ensure successive left-right alternating tail beats and longer swim episodes (Björnfors and El Manira, 2016; Saint-Amant, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Björnfors and El Manira, 2016 and Saint-Amant, 2010, and is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: V2as could very well drive rhythmic tail beats in larval zebrafish while firing tonically.
source: Thus, V2as could very well drive rhythmic tail beats in larval zebrafish while firing tonically.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors based on their modeling results.

claim: The pivotal role of V2as in enabling swimming activity would be to coordinate the many spinal IN populations that generate the patterns of repetitive, left-right alternating tail beats seen in developing zebrafish swimming.
source: If this is the case, then the central role of V2as depends less on their ability to produce a bursting rhythm. Instead, the pivotal role of V2as in enabling swimming activity would be to coordinate the many spinal IN populations that generate the patterns of repetitive, left-right alternating tail beats seen in developing zebrafish swimming (Saint-Amant, 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors based on their modeling results, with a citation to Saint-Amant, 2010.

claim: Burst firing neurons may help to promote the stability of the beat-and-glide pattern.
source: We did find that in simulations where there were only tonic firing neurons, the stability of swimming episode durations started degrading after about 6000 ms. Therefore, burst firing neurons may help to promote the stability of the beat-and-glide pattern.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors based on their modeling results.

claim: Neuromodulation may serve as a mechanism that permits V2as, or other spinal neurons, to toggle between tonic and burst firing through neuromodulation.
source: Neuromodulation may serve as a mechanism that permits V2as, or other spinal neurons, to toggle between tonic and burst firing through neuromodulation.
evidence: The claim is a speculation by the authors.

claim: Blocking D4 dopamine receptors at 3 dpf prevents the transition from burst to beat-and-glide swimming, suggesting that dopamine from supraspinal sources plays a role in setting the beat-and-glide phenotype by shortening swimming episode duration.
source: Blocking D4 dopamine receptors at 3 dpf prevents the transition from burst to beat-and-glide swimming (Lambert et al., 2012), suggesting that dopamine from supraspinal sources plays a role in setting the beat-and-glide phenotype by shortening swimming episode duration.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lambert et al., 2012.

claim: Paired recordings of diencephalospinal dopaminergic neurons and spinal MNs during swimming show that these two populations often burst together.
source: Paired recordings of diencephalospinal dopaminergic neurons and spinal MNs during swimming show that these two populations often burst together (Jay et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jay et al., 2015.

claim: At 6–7 dpf, activation of D1 dopamine receptors increases the recruitment of slow MNs to increase swimming speed.
source: Later in development at 6–7 dpf, activation of D1 dopamine receptors increases the recruitment of slow MNs to increase swimming speed (Jha and Thirumalai, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jha and Thirumalai, 2020.

claim: Serotonin has been found to either increase motor output by decreasing inter-episode intervals in intact larval zebrafish.
source: The neuromodulator serotonin (5-HT) has been found to either increase motor output by decreasing inter-episode intervals in intact larval zebrafish (Brustein and Drapeau, 2005; Brustein et al., 2003) or decrease swimming frequency or burst firing in spinalized larvae and adult zebrafish (Gabriel et al., 2009; Montgomery et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brustein and Drapeau, 2005 and Brustein et al., 2003.

claim: Serotonin has been found to decrease swimming frequency or burst firing in spinalized larvae and adult zebrafish.
source: The neuromodulator serotonin (5-HT) has been found to either increase motor output by decreasing inter-episode intervals in intact larval zebrafish (Brustein and Drapeau, 2005; Brustein et al., 2003) or decrease swimming frequency or burst firing in spinalized larvae and adult zebrafish (Gabriel et al., 2009; Montgomery et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gabriel et al., 2009 and Montgomery et al., 2018.

claim: In the adult zebrafish, serotonin strengthens inhibition to MNs between tail beats and slows down the onset of the depolarization that initiates each successive tail beat.
source: In the adult zebrafish, serotonin strengthens inhibition to MNs between tail beats and slows down the onset of the depolarization that initiates each successive tail beat (Gabriel et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gabriel et al., 2009.

claim: The neuromodulation of intrinsic properties that affect the membrane potential dynamics of spinal neurons could easily modulate locomotor output.
source: Our sensitivity analysis suggests that the neuromodulation of intrinsic properties that affect the membrane potential dynamics of spinal neurons could easily modulate locomotor output.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: Variability in both model parameters and motor output should not necessarily be considered weaknesses of the model but may instead reflect true biological variability.
source: Model parameter variability sometimes increased the variability of motor output (e.g., Figure 10), perhaps indicating a breakdown of the model. However, variability in both model parameters and motor output should not necessarily be considered weaknesses of the model but may instead reflect true biological variability (Marder and Taylor, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marder and Taylor, 2011.

claim: Recordings of swimming characteristics such as episode duration and inter-episode intervals in larval zebrafish show appreciable variation.
source: For instance, recordings of swimming characteristics such as episode duration and inter-episode intervals in larval zebrafish show appreciable variation (Brustein and Drapeau, 2005; Buss and Drapeau, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brustein and Drapeau, 2005 and Buss and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: This is the first model to generate several forms of locomotor movements in developing zebrafish based upon previously described neurons and their connectivity patterns.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first model to generate several forms of locomotor movements in developing zebrafish based upon previously described neurons and their connectivity patterns.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The single coiling model predicts that IC and V0d are coupled together to facilitate the activation of V0ds, which are responsible for the glycinergic SBs observed in spinal neurons at this stage.
source: For instance, the single coiling model predicts that IC and V0d are coupled together to facilitate the activation of V0ds, which are responsible for the glycinergic SBs observed in spinal neurons at this stage (Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001; Tong and McDearmid, 2012).
evidence: The claim is a prediction made by the authors based on their modeling results, with citations to Saint-Amant and Drapeau, 2001 and Tong and McDearmid, 2012.

claim: The V2a to V0v connection would be needed to activate the ipsilateral V0v responsible for the activation of contralateral ICs.
source: The latter connection would be needed to initiate consecutive left-right alternating coils through the activation of contralateral IC neurons, while the former connection would be needed to activate the ipsilateral V0v responsible for the activation of contralateral ICs.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Several of the predictions from the double-coiling model are supported by pharmacological experiments suggesting that blocking glutamatergic transmission in embryonic zebrafish precludes double coiling while blocking glycinergic transmission at that stage promotes multiple coilings.
source: Several of these predictions are supported by pharmacological experiments suggesting that blocking glutamatergic transmission in embryonic zebrafish precludes double coiling while blocking glycinergic transmission at that stage promotes multiple coilings (Knogler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knogler et al., 2014.

claim: Whether delayed contralateral excitation is a conserved mechanism of operation in double coiling and swimming remains to be tested experimentally.
source: Whether delayed contralateral excitation is a conserved mechanism of operation in double coiling and swimming remains to be tested experimentally.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The continued presence of left-right tail beats in simulations where the dI6 population of commissural inhibitory neurons was silenced or in simulations with blockade of glycinergic transmission further underscores the need to test the contributions of V0v neurons to left-right alternation.
source: The continued presence of left-right tail beats in simulations where the dI6 population of commissural inhibitory neurons was silenced or in simulations with blockade of glycinergic transmission further underscores the need to test the contributions of V0v neurons to left-right alternation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The ability of the model to generate beat-and-glide swimming with or without burst firing neurons suggests a possible degeneracy in the operation of spinal swimming circuits of the developing zebrafish.
source: Finally, the ability of our model to generate beat-and-glide swimming with or without burst firing neurons suggests a possible degeneracy in the operation of spinal swimming circuits of the developing zebrafish. This possibility would be consistent with the well-characterized degeneracy of the nervous system, as reinforced by modeling studies where combinations of intrinsic properties or connectivity can generate the same motor output (Goldman et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Goldman et al., 2001 and Taylor et al., 2009.

claim: Many rhythmogenic currents (e.g., NMDA, calcium-dependent potassium currents, and persistent sodium currents) have been implicated in the operation of locomotor circuits of zebrafish.
source: Many rhythmogenic currents (e.g., NMDA, calcium-dependent potassium currents, and persistent sodium currents) have been implicated in the operation of locomotor circuits of zebrafish (Song et al., 2020) and other invertebrate and vertebrate rhythm-generating circuits (Anderson et al., 2012; Golowasch and Marder, 1992; Ryczko et al., 2010; Tazerart et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2020; Anderson et al., 2012; Golowasch and Marder, 1992; Ryczko et al., 2010; Tazerart et al., 2007; Zhong et al., 2007.

claim: Whether the spinal circuits for swimming are degenerate or degeneracy is only exhibited in the modeling remains to be tested experimentally.
source: Whether the spinal circuits for swimming are degenerate or degeneracy is only exhibited in our modeling remains to be tested experimentally.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The operation of the spinal swimming circuit in zebrafish may exhibit degeneracy dependent upon specific environmental or physiological conditions and their resulting neuromodulatory states.
source: The operation of the spinal swimming circuit in zebrafish may exhibit degeneracy dependent upon specific environmental or physiological conditions (Vogelstein et al., 2014) and their resulting neuromodulatory states.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vogelstein et al., 2014.
